office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The district: Garrett-Keyser-Butler Community School District (GKB) serves the city of Garrett and Keyser and Butler townships in DeKalb County. Its schools are J.E. Ober Elementary, Garrett Middle School and Garrett High School [24, 25]. Superintendent Dan Durrwachter reported fall enrollment of 1,636 in January 2026, describing it as a slow decrease over the past few years [26]. Durrwachter, previously assistant superintendent at Peru Community Schools, has led the district since July 1, 2024 under a contract running through June 30, 2027 [27].

Board: five members, each with a residence area. Mark Thrush (president, Butler Township, term ends 12/31/28), Brent Weller (vice president, Keyser Township, 12/31/28), Dottie Fuentes (secretary, Garrett City, 12/31/28), Matt Freeze (Garrett City, 12/31/26) and Luke Ice (at large, 12/31/26) [24]. The 2026 sample ballot for a Keyser Township precinct includes both the at-large and the City of Garrett races, so voters across the district elect these seats [28]. In January 2026 the board re-elected Thrush as president over Freeze, 4-1 [29].

Seats on the 2026 ballot: two seats, one per race, matching the state list's "vote for 1" [28, 6]. At large: incumbent Luke Ice is running against Steven James Kelham [24, 6]. City of Garrett: the seat held by Matt Freeze, who is not on the ballot. Brianne F. Haiflich, Cherrie L. B. Wells and Travis Lee Gaar are running for it [24, 6, 28]. In 2022 Ice challenged and Freeze ran for the open city seat, and both now hold those seats [30, 24].
Party labels: all five candidates are listed as Nonpartisan on the state list [6].

New elementary school: in July 2025 the board approved lease, construction-fund and general obligation bond resolutions to build a new J.E. Ober Elementary [31]. Ground was broken May 22, 2026, and interior demolition was under way by July 2026 [25, 32]. During construction, fifth graders are moving to the middle school for two years starting in fall 2026 [33].

Budget and SEA 1: the board held hearings Sept. 22, 2025 and adopted the 2026 budget on Oct. 27, 2025. It totals $24.5 million, with an estimated $2.9 million maximum operations levy and an estimated $317,400 property-tax-cap credit [34, 35]. In March 2026 the board hired Policy Analytics for an $11,000 parcel study. Durrwachter said the study would include the effects of Senate Bill 1 on property taxes and operations funding, and would help time the bond sales for the elementary project [33]. In July 2026 the board used a state supplemental homestead credit to move $131,296 from debt service to operations, which Durrwachter tied to SEA 1 revenue losses [32].

Other items: at the Sept. 22, 2025 hearing a retired teacher questioned the district's decision to end a swim-instruction partnership with the local JAM Center [34]. New principals were hired for the high school (Kyle Wood, April 2026) and J.E. Ober (Kyle George, May 2026) [36, 37]. The district also resurfaced its track in 2026, and the work was nearly finished by mid-July [33, 32].
Forums: no 2026 candidate forum or questionnaire was found. In 2022, Garrett High School students held a town hall for that year's candidates, which KPC Media covered [30].

candidates.summary: Incumbent at-large member, first elected in 2022 after challenging incumbent Tami Best; listed as Nonpartisan [24, 30, 6].
background: In 2022 KPC Media described him as a parent of students in Garrett schools and a coach of youth teams [30].
He was elected secretary of the district's board of finance in January 2026 and serves on the school calendar committee [26, 33].
path_to_ballot: Listed on the state ballot list as Nonpartisan for the at-large seat [6, 28].

items: At the 2022 candidate town hall, KPC Media reported that he suggested "trimming the fat" from the budget to increase funds [30].
In 2022 he said he saw no major program gap, would build on existing programs, and agreed that a personal finance course covering taxes and accounting could be a good addition [30].

on_incumbent: In Oct. 2025, at his request, a $96,617 Dekko Foundation grant for teacher training in child development was pulled from the list of accepted grants pending further discussion. Fellow member Dottie Fuentes objected, saying teachers' development was being put on hold, and argued the matter did not belong in an executive session. Ice replied that "it probably should be an executive session" and said he was open to questions [35].
On the 2027-28 and 2028-29 calendars approved in March 2026, he said, "It's not perfect but its pretty good" [33].
In 2022, as a challenger, he praised the then-board, superintendent and administrators: "You've done a great job" [30].
plans: In 2022 he said, "We are a good school system — I think we can be a great school system" [30].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign finance reports were found in fetched sources.
gaps: No 2026 campaign statement, website or questionnaire was found; his positions above are from 2022.

candidates.summary: Candidate for the City of Garrett seat now held by Matt Freeze, who is not on the ballot; she also ran for the city seat in 2022. Listed as Nonpartisan [6, 24, 30].
background: In 2022 KPC Media described her as an accountant and a parent of students in Garrett schools who volunteered in many parts of the school [30].
path_to_ballot: Listed on the state ballot list as Nonpartisan for the City of Garrett seat [6, 28].
She ran for the city seat in 2022, when Matt Freeze, who holds it now, was also a candidate [30, 24].

items: In 2022 she said she would work to make the district's dollars "go as far as they can," as KPC Media paraphrased her [30].
In 2022 she said GKB gives students a strong foundation and suggested improving true college readiness, questioning whether students earning dual credits are ready for college-level courses [30].
